excerpt: In one of his lectures, Spanish scholar Carlos Madrid underscores the need for further exploration of primary sources, recognizing the 19th century as a pivotal period in NMI history. Emphasizing an island-centric…
author: HOUSE OF TAGA DESK
bodyText:
The nineteenth century was a pivotal one for the islands, according to Carlos Madrid, a Spanish scholar whose lecture I had the pleasure of listening to years ago when I lived on Saipan. He thinks too few people have read the primary sources. He would like the history told from the islands outward, and when it is, a good deal turns up. Carolinians came to settle and trade. Chamorros resettled Saipan. Smallpox reached Guam in 1856. Whalers did well for a while and then didn't. Spain, which had held the islands for two centuries, extended its rule to the Northern Marianas.

Madrid divides the century at 1850 and 1885, so the periods run 1804 to 1850, 1850 to 1885, and 1885 to 1899.

The trade between the Carolines and the Marianas had been interrupted when the colonizers arrived. It reopened in 1804, when Luis de Torres made the crossing on an American ship. Saipan began to fill up again, and Carolinians kept arriving. The French expedition under Louis-Claude de Saulces de Freycinet spent three months in the Marianas gathering ethnographic and geographic data. The whalers followed in the 1820s and stayed into the 1860s. Guam supplied them. It also supplied the galleons running between Acapulco and Manila until that trade was interrupted in 1815.

The government was local and small. The smallest unit was the barangay, headed by a cabeza. A cabeza could be elected gobernadorcillo, which made him head of the town and its judge. As in the Philippines, only men could vote or hold office. The seat of authority was the Casa Real. The one on Rota is the oldest standing building in the Marianas. On Saipan, the site is now occupied by a Jollibee.

Spanish administration rested on the Church and on the law. The authority for the first went back to the sixteenth-century Patronato Real, which allowed Christianity to be spread. A Jesuit school ran on Guam until the Jesuits were expelled. Religious teaching went on after that anyway.

Smallpox arrived on Guam in 1856, probably on a ship from the Philippines. Quarantine laws were on the books and were loosely observed. Madrid says the epidemic killed sixty percent of the population. In the 1870s, after the Cavite Mutiny of 1872, exiles and political prisoners were sent to the Marianas. Food was already scarce, and tempers over it were short.

By 1885 the United States, Japan, and Germany had all begun to consider the Marianas as a possible colony. The Treaty of Paris settled it in 1899. Guam, along with the Philippines, passed to the United States. The Northern Marianas went to Germany.
title: 19th century Marianas
